etymology: A divine title: “the Holy One of Israel” for the LORD, and “the Holy One of God” for Christ; from the Hebrew qadosh, holy, set apart.
biblical_def: The Holy One is a title of God and of Christ that gathers up the awful purity and separateness of the divine nature. Isaiah, who saw the seraphim cry Holy, holy, holy, uses “the Holy One of Israel” some thirty times as his favorite name for the LORD—the God whose holiness both terrifies and saves, the Redeemer of His people: I am the LORD thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour. The title passes to Christ in the New Testament. The unclean spirit, recognizing Him, cried, I know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God; and Peter confessed, Thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God. Above all, the sixteenth Psalm, fulfilled in the resurrection, declares of Him: thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption—the body of the Holy One was not given over to decay but raised in glory, as both Peter and Paul preached. The dictionary reads the Holy One as the title that joins the holiness of God to the person of Christ: the thrice-holy LORD of Isaiah’s vision and the spotless Holy One of God whom death could not corrupt, the sinless Saviour in whom the holy God draws near to redeem an unholy people without ceasing to be holy.
webster_summary: A divine title—“the Holy One of Israel” for the LORD and “the Holy One of God” for Christ—the sinless Saviour whose body death could not corrupt.
webster_full: HOLY ONE, a title of God and of Christ, the awful purity of the divine nature.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the age that cannot bear the holiness of God prefers a tame deity; the Holy One is the thrice-holy LORD and the sinless Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift to name is the sentimental reduction of God to mere kindness, stripping away the holiness that the title Holy One enshrines. The age prefers a tame and tolerant deity who makes no man tremble; but the God of Scripture is the thrice-holy LORD before whom Isaiah was undone, the Holy One of Israel whose holiness is a consuming fire. To lose the holiness of God is to lose the gravity of sin, the necessity of the cross, and the wonder of salvation; for it is precisely the Holy One who stoops to be the Saviour. A God who is all kindness and no holiness is an idol.

The principle to recover is the holiness of God joined to the person of Christ. The same title that names the awful purity of the LORD names the spotless Christ, the Holy One of God whom even demons confessed and whose body the grave could not corrupt. The gospel is the marvel that the Holy One should bear the sin of the unholy without ceasing to be holy—made sin for us who knew no sin, that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him. The Holy One redeems by His holiness, not in spite of it.

etymology: From Hebrews 7:2, the interpretation of Melchizedek’s name as “King of righteousness”; a title of Christ the righteous King.
biblical_def: King of righteousness is the interpretation the epistle to the Hebrews gives of the name Melchizedek—first by interpretation King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is King of peace—and it is a title that finds its fulfillment in Christ. Melchizedek, the priest-king of Salem who blessed Abraham and received his tithe, was a type of the Lord Jesus, who is both King and Priest, both righteous and the giver of peace. The order is itself a gospel: first righteousness, then peace; for there is no peace with God except on the ground of righteousness, and Christ secures the peace by establishing the righteousness. Jeremiah foretold the messianic King under the very name: this is his name whereby he shall be called, THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS. Isaiah saw a King who shall reign in righteousness; the Psalm hails the messianic throne, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre. The dictionary reads King of righteousness as a title of Christ in His threefold work: He is righteous in His own person, the spotless King; He is the LORD our righteousness, who provides for His people the righteousness they lack; and He reigns in righteousness, ruling His kingdom with a right sceptre and bringing in everlasting righteousness at the last.
webster_summary: From Hebrews 7:2, the meaning of Melchizedek’s name; a title of Christ the righteous King—righteous in person, the LORD our righteousness, who reigns with a right sceptre.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the age would have a king of peace without righteousness; Scripture sets righteousness first, the only ground of true peace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error the title rebukes is the longing for peace without righteousness—a sentimental hope that God will grant peace and reconciliation while leaving sin unjudged and righteousness unsecured. But the order of Melchizedek’s name is fixed and gospel-shaped: first King of righteousness, and after that King of peace. There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked; the peace that Christ gives rests upon the righteousness He establishes. To seek the peace while despising the righteousness is to want the fruit without the root, and it ends not in peace but in a false and fatal calm.

The principle to recover is the righteous King who secures peace by righteousness. Christ is the King of righteousness in every sense: righteous in His own spotless person; the LORD our righteousness, who imputes to His people the righteousness they could never earn; and the reigning King who rules with a right sceptre and shall bring in everlasting righteousness. Because He is first the King of righteousness, He can be the King of peace; His blood satisfies justice, and on that ground He speaks peace to His people and reigns over them in righteousness for ever.

etymology: The second of the two states of Christ; from the Latin exaltare, to lift up—His resurrection, ascension, session, and return in glory.
biblical_def: The exaltation of Christ is the second of His two estates—the lifting up that followed His humiliation—and it comprises His resurrection from the dead, His ascension into heaven, His session at the right hand of the Father, and His coming again in glory to judge the world. The great hymn of Philippians sets the two states together: He humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross; wherefore God also hath highly exalted Him, and given Him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow. Having by Himself purged our sins, He sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high; being by the right hand of God exalted, He poured out the promised Spirit at Pentecost. The exaltation is the Father’s public vindication of the Son’s finished work: the same Jesus who was crucified in weakness God raised, enthroned, and crowned with glory and honor, declaring Him both Lord and Christ. The dictionary reads the exaltation of Christ as the triumphant answer of God to the cross: the humbled Servant exalted to universal dominion, reigning now at the Father’s right hand as Prophet, Priest, and King, until He has put all enemies under His feet and every knee bows at His name.
webster_summary: The second estate of Christ—His resurrection, ascension, session at God’s right hand, and return in glory—the Father’s vindication of the Son’s finished work.

corruption_summary: Liberalism keeps a crucified teacher but empties the resurrection and ascension of literal truth; Scripture proclaims the bodily-risen, ascended, reigning Christ exalted to universal dominion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the liberal evacuation of Christ’s exaltation—keeping a noble crucified teacher while reducing His resurrection to a symbol of enduring influence and His ascension to a myth, so that the exalted Christ becomes a feeling in the disciples’ hearts rather than the Lord enthroned in heaven. But the apostles preached a literal exaltation: the same body that was crucified was raised, the same Jesus ascended visibly, and He sits now at the right hand of God, whence He poured out the Spirit they saw and heard at Pentecost. Empty the exaltation of its reality, and the cross is a defeat and the gospel a fond memory.

The principle to recover is the bodily-risen, ascended, and reigning Christ. The exaltation is the Father’s vindication of the Son: God highly exalted the One who humbled Himself, gave Him the name above every name, and seated Him in dominion until every knee shall bow. He reigns now as Prophet, Priest, and King, ever living to make intercession, ruling over all, and He shall come again in the glory of that exaltation to judge the quick and the dead. The crucified Saviour is the crowned Lord.

etymology: The triumph of Christ over the devil promised in Genesis 3:15 and accomplished at the cross; the crushing of the serpent’s head.
biblical_def: Christ’s victory over Satan is the great theme that runs from the first promise of the gospel to the last vision of Revelation: the woman’s Seed should bruise the serpent’s head, and at the cross He did. Through His sinless life the Lord met and overcame every temptation of the devil; through His death He overthrew him, for as the children are partakers of flesh and blood He likewise took part of the same, that through death He might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. The cross, which seemed the devil’s triumph, was his ruin: having spoiled principalities and powers, Christ made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it. The Lord saw Satan as lightning fall from heaven; the strong man was bound and his house spoiled. The victory, won at the cross, is applied to the saints, who overcome the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, and shall see the God of peace bruise Satan under their feet shortly. The dictionary reads Christ’s victory over Satan as the decisive triumph of redemption: the serpent’s head is crushed, his works destroyed, his power over death broken, and his final doom sealed—already accomplished at Calvary, already shared by faith, and to be consummated when Satan is cast for ever into the lake of fire.
webster_summary: The triumph of Christ over the devil promised in Genesis 3:15 and won at the cross—destroying him that had the power of death and spoiling principalities openly.

corruption_summary: The age denies the devil’s reality, emptying the victory of meaning, while charismatic “spiritual warfare” presumes a power the saints wield only in Christ; the triumph is His, won at the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors press against the doctrine. The first is the modern denial of Satan’s reality, which dissolves the devil into a symbol of impersonal evil and so empties Christ’s victory of its object—there is no triumph if there is no enemy. The second is the opposite excess of much “spiritual warfare” teaching, which has believers binding and rebuking demons by formula and presumes a personal authority over the devil that Scripture never grants the saint apart from Christ. The victory is Christ’s, won decisively at the cross; the believer shares it by faith and resists the devil by the Word, not by techniques of his own.

The principle to recover is the finished and decisive triumph of Christ. At the cross, which the powers thought their victory, He destroyed him that had the power of death and spoiled principalities openly; the serpent’s head, promised crushed in Eden, was crushed. The saints overcome the accuser not by their own strength but by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, resisting the devil steadfast in the faith. The war is real, but its outcome is settled: the God of peace shall bruise Satan under His people’s feet, and the enemy’s doom is the lake of fire.

etymology: The childhood and youth of the Lord Jesus at Nazareth, chiefly the scene of the boy in the temple (Luke 2:40–52).
biblical_def: The boyhood of Christ is the hidden growth of the Lord Jesus from infancy to manhood at Nazareth, of which the Gospels give one luminous scene: the boy of twelve in the temple at Jerusalem. Scripture says the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him—a true and real human development, the eternal Son growing as a boy. At twelve, lingering in the temple after the feast, He was found among the doctors, both hearing them and asking them questions, and all that heard Him were astonished at His understanding. To His mother’s gentle reproach He gave His first recorded words: How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business?—the dawning consciousness of His unique Sonship and mission. Then He went down with them and was subject unto them, the perfect Son honoring His earthly parents; and Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man. The dictionary reads the boyhood of Christ as a window into the reality of the incarnation: the Son of God was truly a boy, who grew, learned, obeyed, and was subject to His parents, sinless in every stage, fulfilling all righteousness even in childhood—true God and true man from the cradle, growing toward the cross.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors touch the boyhood of Christ. The first is the apocryphal one: the so-called infancy gospels, rejected by the church, fill His childhood with grotesque and fanciful miracles—the boy striking playmates dead or making clay birds fly—legends that contradict the sober Gospel record and the sinless character of the Lord. The second is the modern denial of the reality of His growth, as though true deity could not truly learn or develop; but Luke plainly says He increased in wisdom and stature. The canonical Gospels give one restrained, luminous scene, and we are not to add to it the inventions of pious fancy.

The principle to recover is the reality of the incarnation from the cradle. The eternal Son was truly a boy—He grew, waxed strong, was filled with wisdom, asked and answered questions, and was subject to His parents—yet without sin, fulfilling all righteousness even in childhood. His first recorded words reveal the dawning consciousness of His Father’s business, and His obedience at Nazareth fulfilled the fifth commandment perfectly on our behalf. He was true God and true man at every stage, the obedient Son whose whole life, boyhood included, was a sinless righteousness reckoned to His people.

etymology: The phase of the Lord’s public ministry centered in Galilee, chiefly about Capernaum and the sea of Galilee.
biblical_def: The Galilean ministry is the great central phase of the Lord’s public work, carried out in the northern region of Galilee—about the sea of Galilee and based at Capernaum—where He preached the kingdom, called His first disciples, worked many of His mighty miracles, and gave much of His teaching, including the Sermon on the Mount. After John was cast into prison, Jesus came into Galilee preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God and saying, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. He went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness among the people. That He should begin there fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy of Galilee of the nations: the people which sat in darkness saw great light, and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up. From the fishermen of its lake He called Peter and Andrew, James and John; among its villages He fed the multitudes and stilled the storm. The dictionary reads the Galilean ministry as the season of the kingdom’s proclamation in word and work: the Light shining first upon a despised and half-heathen region, the King announcing His kingdom, gathering His disciples, and authenticating His message by mighty deeds, before He set His face to go up to Jerusalem and the cross.
webster_summary: The central phase of the Lord’s ministry in Galilee, based at Capernaum; preaching the kingdom, calling disciples, and working miracles—the great Light shining on Galilee of the nations.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the kingdom He preached is reduced to a social program; He proclaimed repentance and the reign of God, authenticated by miracle.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift to name is the reduction of the kingdom Jesus preached in Galilee to a merely social or political program—a movement of liberation and human flourishing—stripped of its first and central demand. But the Galilean preaching began with a word the social gospel omits: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. The kingdom He announced is the reign of God breaking into the world in His own person, calling men to turn from sin and believe; His miracles were not mere acts of compassion but signs authenticating the King and His message. To keep the compassion and discard the call to repentance is to lose the gospel of the kingdom He preached.

The principle to recover is the kingdom proclaimed in word and work. The Galilean ministry is the season of the King announcing His reign—preaching the gospel of the kingdom, calling sinners to repentance and faith, gathering disciples, and confirming His word by healing all manner of sickness. It fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy that the great Light would shine first on despised Galilee of the nations, a foretaste of the gospel going to the Gentiles. The King who shone His light on Galilee called men then, as now, to repent and receive His reign.

etymology: The bringing of the infant Jesus to the temple to be presented to the Lord, forty days after His birth (Luke 2:22–38).
biblical_def: The presentation of Christ is the bringing of the infant Jesus to the temple in Jerusalem, forty days after His birth, that He might be presented to the Lord according to the law of Moses, and that His mother might offer the appointed sacrifice of purification—a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, the offering of the poor. The scene is rich with gospel light. The aged and devout Simeon, to whom it had been revealed that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ, took the child in his arms and blessed God: Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: for mine eyes have seen thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; a light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel. He warned Mary that this child was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and that a sword should pierce through her own soul. Anna the prophetess, a widow of great age who departed not from the temple, gave thanks likewise and spoke of Him to all that looked for redemption in Jerusalem. The dictionary reads the presentation of Christ as the meeting of the Old Covenant’s waiting saints with the Saviour come at last: the firstborn presented to the Lord, the law fulfilled, and the long-expected salvation, prepared for both Gentile and Jew, beheld and confessed by Simeon and Anna.
webster_summary: The bringing of the infant Jesus to the temple forty days after His birth; the meeting with Simeon and Anna, who beheld the salvation prepared—a light to the Gentiles and the glory of Israel.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The accretion to set aside is the medieval overlaying of this scene with Marian devotion—the feast kept as the “Purification of the Blessed Virgin,” with attention bent toward the mother rather than the Son. But Luke’s account fixes every eye on the child: it is Christ who is presented to the Lord, Christ whom Simeon beheld as the salvation of God, Christ who is the light to the Gentiles and the glory of Israel. Mary’s purification offering is the offering of the poor, and Simeon’s word to her foretells a sword through her own soul—she is a humble worshipper in the scene, not its object.

The principle to recover is the Saviour beheld by the waiting saints. The presentation gathers up the longing of the Old Covenant: Simeon, who waited for the consolation of Israel, and Anna, who spoke of Him to all that looked for redemption, are the faithful remnant whose eyes at last see the salvation of God. The infant fulfills the law as the firstborn presented to the Lord, and is shown to be the salvation prepared before the face of all people—a light for the Gentiles and the glory of Israel. The glory of the scene is wholly Christ’s.

etymology: A title of Christ as the trail-blazing Captain and Author of faith and salvation (Hebrews 2:10; 12:2); the One who leads the way to glory.
biblical_def: Pioneer of faith is a title of Christ drawn from the epistle to the Hebrews, where He is called the author and finisher of our faith and the captain of our salvation—the trail-blazer who goes before His people, opening the way to God and leading the way to glory. He is the author of faith, the One in whom faith begins and on whom it fixes its eye, who for the joy that was set before Him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God; and He is its finisher, who perfects the faith He begins. It became the Father, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings—the Pioneer made complete as Saviour through the very road of suffering He traveled before His people. He is the forerunner entered for us within the veil, the High Priest after the order of Melchizedek; being made perfect, He became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey Him. The dictionary reads the Pioneer of faith as Christ the trail-blazing Captain: the One who, as the eternal Son made man, ran the race of faith before us, blazed the path through suffering and death into glory, entered heaven as our forerunner, and now leads His many sons along the way He opened, perfecting the faith He authored until they are with Him where He is.
webster_summary: A title of Christ as the trail-blazing Captain and Author of faith and salvation; who ran the race before us, opened the way through suffering to glory, and entered as our forerunner.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though “pioneer” may be misread to make Christ a mere example to imitate; He is the Captain who accomplishes the salvation He pioneers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misreading to guard against is the reduction of Christ the Pioneer to a mere moral example—the first and best man of faith whom we are simply to imitate—as though His pioneering were only an inspiring precedent and not an accomplishing work. But the Captain of salvation does not merely show the way; He opens it and brings His people through it. He is the author of our faith, not only its model; the captain who secures the victory, not only its herald; the forerunner who has entered within the veil to bring us after Him. He saves those He leads; He does not merely encourage them.

The principle to recover is Christ as the trail-blazing Captain who accomplishes salvation. As the eternal Son made man He ran the race of faith before us, endured the cross for the joy set before Him, and was made perfect as Saviour through the very sufferings He bore in our place; He entered heaven as our forerunner and High Priest. He is the author of faith and its finisher, beginning and perfecting it in His people. We look unto Jesus not merely to copy Him but to be carried by Him—the Pioneer who blazed the path and leads His many sons home to glory.

etymology: A title of Christ from Isaiah 9:6, “Wonderful, Counsellor”; one who gives wise counsel and direction.
biblical_def: Counsellor is one of the great names given to the messianic child in Isaiah’s prophecy: unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. As Counsellor, Christ is the One in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, the wisdom of God incarnate, who needs no counsellor Himself—for who hath known the mind of the Lord, or who hath been His counsellor?—yet who is given to His people as their unfailing guide. The LORD of hosts, says Isaiah elsewhere, is wonderful in counsel and excellent in working; and Wisdom herself declares, Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom; I am understanding; I have strength. The world, having forsaken the fear of the LORD that is the beginning of wisdom, seeks counsel everywhere but from God, heaping to itself counsellors of the flesh; but the believer’s Counsellor is Christ, who orders the steps of His people, gives wisdom liberally to them that ask, and guides them by His Word and Spirit. The dictionary reads Counsellor as a title of the wisdom and guidance of Christ: the wonderful Counsellor who plans redemption in eternal wisdom, executes it in perfect working, and gives Himself as the all-sufficient guide of His people, against every counsel of the flesh and folly of the age.
webster_summary: A title of Christ from Isaiah 9:6, “Wonderful, Counsellor”; the wisdom of God incarnate and the all-sufficient guide of His people by His Word and Spirit.

corruption_summary: The age seeks counsel everywhere but from God, multiplying counsellors of the flesh; the believer’s Counsellor is Christ, the wisdom of God, who guides by His Word and Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift to name is the modern flight from divine counsel to the counsel of the flesh. Having forsaken the fear of the LORD that is the beginning of wisdom, the age seeks guidance everywhere but from God—in the wisdom of the world, the therapies of the hour, the consensus of experts—heaping to itself counsellors after its own desires. Even much that passes for Christian counsel borrows the categories of secular psychology and loses the sufficiency of the Word. But the LORD asks, who hath been my counsellor? He needs none; and His people need no other guide than the wisdom He gives.

The principle to recover is Christ the Counsellor and the sufficiency of His guidance. The messianic Son is named Wonderful, Counsellor—the very wisdom of God, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, wonderful in counsel and excellent in working. He gives Himself to His people as their unfailing guide, ordering their steps, giving wisdom liberally to them that ask in faith, and leading them by His Word and Spirit. The believer is not left to the counsel of the flesh; he has a wonderful Counsellor, and in Him sound wisdom for every step of the way.

etymology: The principle that the whole of Scripture, Old Testament and New, testifies of Christ (Luke 24:27; John 5:39).
biblical_def: Christ in all Scripture is the principle, taught by the Lord Jesus Himself, that the whole of the written Word—the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms—testifies of Him, so that He is the substance and center of all the Scriptures. On the road to Emmaus, beginning at Moses and all the prophets, He expounded unto the disciples in all the scriptures the things concerning Himself; and to the gathered eleven He said that all things must be fulfilled which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning Him. To the unbelieving He said, Search the scriptures, for in them ye think ye have eternal life, and they are they which testify of me; and, Had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me, for he wrote of me. Thus the promised Seed of Genesis, the Passover lamb, the rock in the wilderness, the suffering Servant of Isaiah, the smitten Shepherd of Zechariah, the Son of man of Daniel, and the King of the Psalms all point to Christ; the Old Testament is the gospel in promise, type, and prophecy, and the New is its fulfillment. The dictionary reads Christ in all Scripture as the unifying key to the Bible: He is the theme of the whole, foreshadowed in the Old and revealed in the New, so that to read the Scriptures rightly is to find Christ in them, from Genesis to Revelation.

corruption_summary: Higher criticism severs the Old Testament from Christ as merely ancient religion, and a flat moralism reads it for examples only; the Lord teaches that all the Scriptures testify of Him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors sever Christ from the Scriptures. The first is the higher-critical reading that treats the Old Testament as merely the evolving religion of ancient Israel, with no genuine prophecy and no real foreshadowing of Christ, so that the connections the New Testament draws are dismissed as creative misreadings. The second is a flat moralism that mines the Old Testament only for examples of behavior—be brave like David, be pure like Joseph—and never finds the Christ to whom every story points. Both miss what the Lord Himself taught: the Scriptures testify of Him, and Moses wrote of Him.

The principle to recover is Christ as the unifying theme and substance of the whole Bible. He expounded in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself and declared that the law, the prophets, and the psalms all speak of Him. The promised Seed, the Passover lamb, the bronze serpent, the suffering Servant, the smitten Shepherd, the Son of man, the royal Bridegroom of the Psalms—all foreshadow Him; the Old Testament is the gospel in promise and type, the New its fulfillment. To read the Scriptures rightly is to find Christ in them, for of Him they testify from first to last.
